en: In order to show the names and characteristics of the seven [deities] through the absorption of the twenty-four yoginīs who reside in the Saṃvara maṇḍala, he says "Listen," and so forth. The word *tu* indicates a distinction. Regarding the phrase "in seven ways": the meaning is that the forms of the twenty-four yoginīs—who are the retinue of the Vidyārāja to be described—have been absorbed into these [seven].

In this regard, the instruction is as follows: Mahāvīryā, Cakravartinī, Mahābalā, and Suvīrā—these four are Yāminī; Rūpikā is she herself. Cakravarmiṇī, Śauṇḍinī, Khaṇḍarohā, and Cakravegā—these are Cumbikā; Trāsinī is she herself. Khagānanā, Hayakarṇā, Subhadrā, and Śyāmādevī—these are Lāmā; Kānarī (or Kānanī) and Raudrī are she herself. Surābhakṣī, Vāyuvegā, Mahābhairavā, and Airāvatī—these are Parāvṛttā; Bhīmā and Caṇḍālī are she herself.

Drumacchāyā, Laṅkeśvarī, Kharvarī, Vīramatī with Vālikā, Saṃcārā, and Āyurbhakṣaṇī; Mahānāsā, Prabhāvatī, Caṇḍākṣī, Pracaṇḍā, Anivarttikā, and she herself as Bhāsurā; again Vīramatī as the seventh, who is Aihikī, and she herself as Āyurbhakṣaṇī, and Kānanī.

He states the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the *rūpikā* and others in their respective order, beginning with "not detached" (*avirakta*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "practiced by the non-dual hero" (*vīrādvayasevitā*): she is fit for dalliance (*rantuyogyā*), practiced by the hero (*vīra*), that is, the practitioner of the vow (*saṃvarayogin*), who acts as the non-dual. Her breath is otherwise, serving as an indicator of desire. Furthermore, she is *bhairava*, meaning terrifying. For this very reason, she is called *rāmā* because she delights (*ramate*). Due to the substitution of the letter *l* for *r*, she is *lāmā*. "She should terrify" means that upon seeing her, boars and other animals are struck with fear.

*Parāvṛtā* is that [state] from which others turn back (*parāvartante*). *Sabālikā* means accompanied by children (*bāla*), where "children" refers to moving toward one side (*balanam ekato gamanam*). *Udvigne* means when there is agitation (*udvega*). *Anivartikā* is so called because there is no returning (*nivṛtti*) from it. The word "suddenly" (*akasmāt*) is to be connected with the actions such as laughing and so forth. *Aihikī* means she who stays for a long time in this place. She is called *Yogamātṛ* because she is conducive to yoga. The description beginning with "laughing" (*prahasitā*) and so forth is the characteristic of Vajravārāhī on the eighth [day]. Thus it is said in the *Caturyoginīsaṃpuṭatantra*:
In the *Caturyoginīsaṃpuṭa*, the eight [yoginīs] are remembered as follows: Rūpikā, Cumbikā, Lāmā, Parāvṛtā, Sabālikā,
Anivartikā, Aihikī, and Vajrīṇī as the eighth.
The first is the sealing mudrā, the second is the heart-piercing,
the third is the deluding mudrā, and the fourth is likewise the raising-up;
the fifth is the dancing mudrā, and the sixth is the slaying.
The seventh is the Bhakṣaṇī Mudrā, and the eighth is certainly the Utthāpanī.
Bhāsurā, Kāminī, and Vārāhī is considered the eighth.

The fang is the tusk of a boar. The eight mudrās, beginning with the skull-bowl, correspond respectively to the eight yoginīs. Although the mudrā is merely drawn in the house, it constitutes the defining characteristic [of the deity]. In some places, the reading "seventh" occurs due to a scribe's error.
(Note: This variant reading is judged to be a scribal error.)

One who is skilled in the union of emptiness and compassion should characterize the innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*) as the "performance" (*vidhāna*), by means of these female forms (*rūpikā*) who are marked [with signs], together with the *saṃpuṭa* and through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). The "worldly mothers" (*kaṭaputanya*) are the supramundane mothers such as Rūpikā and the others; their "sign" (*cihna*) and "characteristic mark" (*lakṣaṇa*)—the skull and so forth—are the "sign-seals" (*cihnamudrā*). The chapter that designates them is likewise so called. Their feminine gender is like [the expression] "introduce eight women," and so forth.
The fourteenth mañjarī in the Āmnāyamañjarī, the commentary on the Śrīsampuṭa.
